title: Singers in the old bands, readers, and the work and halls then and now
summary: Band members sang, Chris Kelly's band could not read but worked steadily, and he contrasts plentiful halls then with few places now.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Managers, bookers and the business of getting work

blocks.x: You see? But them time they wanted to see all that music there. If you didn't have that band there, you didn't have no band.
No two-three pieces. Did you have any singers at all, hadn't in the old days?

Well, most of the band, people would sing with the band, the man who'd lead, you see. The trumpet player and sometimes the guitar player. Sometimes the piano player, he'd sing what he know about a number. That's how it went. But they never had no regular singers unless you go to the entertainers when they had to have, and then you had to be a first class musician to play in the entertainer because they used to, sometimes the singers would put the music on. You take like Buddy Pitti and them brothers, they wouldn't play in that, you know, unless they had a reading man with them. Well, if you play a job with a band and didn't have no reading, and you as a trumpet player didn't know a note, and you as a clarinet player didn't have a note, and the trombone player didn't know a note, well then you didn't have nobody to pick up on that stuff. But if you had a clarinet player to pick it up, well you could go on with him. If you had a saxophone player also to pick it up, well the trumpet player could go on with him. That's what they'd make a pretty second behind him, and he could play too. See? But you take them time, if you had to have one man and a couple of men in the band read, because the trumpets hardly know, like them fellas, you know, Chris Ketner, they never had no kind of music. But still in all they made money at that time. And they got them jobs every Saturday and Sunday and on the week they was working all the time. They didn't have nothing to do, they didn't do nothing but that. And they could, you know, they had enough money to have a good time in the day, they didn't have nothing to do. And that night go to work, they had big dinners, and all of them be around the table for the big dinners and rent in this yard, they had a big yard. All of them would get around, all of them punch, all of them musicians would come there and get around the table and eat car, where are they all on Monday, see? Because they'd play so hard on Fridays and Saturdays and Sunday like that. At that time, and sometime in the week, and at some time they'd have weddings and things, they'd play all such as things like hall, like the cops like to St. Giles, what you call that, that cut like hall there, or St. Catron, where they used to play all in there too, you see? So them halls used to have them going because they had plenty of places to play. And for the bands they had then, they didn't have much, they had a lot of halls and no bands, you see? Then, at that time, because they had, look at the halls they had, now look at the halls we got now to play. See, different? I mean, look at the bands we got, we ain't got no place to play. Unless you go on the outskirts and them cabarets and them ballroom, they all got a dance hall in the back now. Well, very seldom you can play that on Friday, Saturday, and Sunday. Sometimes you play that Friday and Saturday, they don't want you on Sunday because the people got to go to work, they don't have but three people in the play. But in the country you have plenty of people in the play. That's why a lot of them boys go in the country, that's why this boy he always go around on the other side of the river for all them ballrooms and things around there. Like, what's the name? Marura and them fellas. We used to give dances in Sue's Berry. I used to play up in there too, and colored people. Oh yeah. And Sue's Berry. Marura. Yeah, Marura. Mm-hm.
